{{Short description|American space and exotic matter physicist}}
[[File:Raymond Jeanloz at CTBTO Science and Technology conference.jpg|thumb|Jeanloz in 2011]]
'''Raymond Jeanloz''' is a professor of [[earth science|Earth]] and [[planetary science]] (EPS) and [[Astronomy]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Raymond Jeanloz |url=https://eps.berkeley.edu/people/raymond-jeanloz |website=Earth & Planetary Science}}</ref> Educated at the [[California Institute of Technology]], [[Amherst College]] and at [[Deep Springs College]],<ref name="PSU"/> his research contributions have been fundamental to understanding of the composition of the Earth and the behavior of materials under high temperatures and pressures.<ref name="aps"/> Jeanloz has created tools and experiments that enable him to recreate and study deep interior conditions in a laboratory setting,<ref name="DSC" />  He is working with colleagues to investigate the conditions inside [[supergiant]] [[exoplanet]]s.<ref name=astrobio2007/>  

Jeanloz has chaired the National Research Council Board on Earth Sciences and Resources.<ref name="Hoover" /> He is a co-editor of the ''[[Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences]]''<ref name="Jeanloz">{{cite journal |last1=Jeanloz |first1=Raymond |last2=Freeman |first2=Katherine H. |title=Introduction |journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences |date=30 May 2014 |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=annurev–ea–42-051214-100001 |doi=10.1146/annurev-ea-42-051214-100001 |bibcode=2014AREPS..42.....J |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-ea-42-051214-100001 |access-date=15 September 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and serves on the Board of Directors of [[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Our Board of Directors |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/about/our-team |website=Annual Reviews |access-date=29 July 2024}}</ref>

Jeanloz is also active in connecting science and policy in areas including international policy, resources and the environment, and science education.<ref name="DSC"/><ref name="Fundamental"/> He has been particularly prominent in informing national and international security and nuclear weapons policy,<ref name="Fundamental">{{cite book |title=Fundamental Research in High Energy Density Science|chapter=Committee biographies |date=1 June 2023 |publisher=National Academies Press |doi=10.17226/26728 |isbn=978-0-309-69414-8  |language=en}}</ref> chairing the [[Committee on International Security and Arms Control]] at the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="fas" /> In 2009 he received the [[Leo Szilard Lectureship Award]] from the [[American Physical Society]] for "contributions to development of sound public policy for nuclear weapons management and nuclear non-proliferation."<ref name="aps"/> Jeanloz became an [[Annenberg Foundation|Annenberg]] Distinguished Visiting Fellow at [[Stanford University]]'s [[Hoover Institution]] in 2012.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.hoover.org/profiles/raymond-jeanloz | title=Raymond Jeanloz: Annenberg Distinguished Visiting Fellow | date= | website=Hoover Institution  |publisher=Stanford University | access-date=7 December 2018}}</ref>

==Education==
Raymond Jeanloz is one of four children of [[Roger W. Jeanloz]], a professor in biological chemistry and molecular pharmacology at [[Harvard Medical School]], and his wife Dorothea.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Marquard |first1=Bryan |title=Roger W. Jeanloz, Harvard professor who traveled the world; at 89 |url=https://archive.boston.com/news/globe/obituaries/articles/2007/09/28/roger_w_jeanloz_harvard_professor_who_traveled_the_world_at_89/ |access-date=9 December 2018 |work=Boston Globe |publisher=Boston.com |date=28 September 2007}}</ref> Raymond Jeanloz grew up in [[Massachusetts]] and spent two years at [[Deep Springs College]], located in the [[Deep Springs Valley]]<ref name="PSU">{{cite web |title=Raymond Jeanloz {{!}} Earth 520: Plate Tectonics and People: Foundations of Solid Earth Science |url=https://www.e-education.psu.edu/earth520/node/1800 |website=Penn State University |access-date=26 July 2024}}</ref> between the [[White Mountains (California)|White Mountains]] and [[Inyo Mountains]] in [[California]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lustig |first1=L. K. |title=Clastic sedimentation in Deep Springs Valley, California |date=1965 |publisher=United States Department of the Interior, Geological Survey |location=Washington |doi=10.3133/pp352F  |language=en}}</ref>  His initial interests were in comparative literature and music. While he had some early exposure to geology, his interest in that field developed late in his undergraduate program.<ref name="Zierler"/> Having also tried [[Hampshire College]]<ref name="DSC"/><ref name="Carmichael"/> and taken a "gap period" of several months, Jeanloz  completed his B.A. in geology at [[Amherst College]] in Massachusetts in 1975.<ref name="Macarthur">{{cite web |title=Raymond Jeanloz |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/class-of-1988/raymond-jeanloz |website=Macarthur Foundation |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Zierler">{{cite web |last1=Zierler |first1=David |title=Raymond Jeanloz (PhD '79), Earth and Planetary Scientist |url=https://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews-updates/raymond-jeanloz |website=Caltech Heritage Project |access-date=26 July 2024 |language=en |date=24 August 2022}}</ref>   

Jeanloz applied to the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech) in part because of the [[Caltech Seismological Laboratory]]. His thesis advisor at Caltech was [[Thomas J. Ahrens]]. Jeanloz credits Ahrens and others for their mentorship and support, in helping him to learn about areas where he lacked scientific background and in encouraging him to explore new areas of research.<ref name="Zierler"/> In 1979, Jeanloz received his Ph.D. from Caltech<ref name="Macarthur"/> for the thesis ''Physics of mantle and core minerals'' (1979).<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Jeanloz |first1=Raymond |title=Physics of Mantle and Core Minerals |date=1980 |publisher=California Institute of Technology |doi=10.7907/dzss-k041 |bibcode=1980PhDT.........3J |url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/16138/ |language=en}}</ref>

==Career==
Jeanloz joined the faculty at [[Harvard University]] in 1979,<ref name="DSC"/> working at the intersection of [[materials science]] and physics.<ref name="Zierler"/>  He taught there until 1981.<ref name="DSC">{{cite news |title=The Benefits of a Life of Science: RAYMOND JEANLOZ '70 |url=https://www.deepsprings.edu/sg/wp-content/uploads/2015_AnnualReport.pdf |access-date=26 July 2024 |work=DEEP SPRINGS COLLEGE ANNUAL REPORT 2015 |date=2015}}</ref> In 1982,<ref name="CV">{{cite web |title=Raymond JEANLOZ |url=https://live-astronomy-web.pantheon.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/24/rj-short-cv-08-14.pdf |website=Department of Astronomy, University of California at Berkeley |access-date=29 July 2024}}</ref> he moved to the [[University of California, Berkeley]] where he became a professor of [[earth science|Earth]] and [[planetary science]] and of [[Astronomy]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Medicine |first1=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and |last2=Sciences |first2=Division on Engineering and Physical |last3=Protection |first3=Committee on National Security Space Defense and |title=National Security Space Defense and Protection: Public Report |date=30 August 2016 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-44751-5 |page=51 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WbaDDQAAQBAJ&dq=jeanloz++planetary+interiors&pg=PA51 |access-date=29 July 2024 |language=en}}</ref> 

Jeanloz is a member of the National Academy of Sciences. He advises the US Government, the University of California and its national laboratories on a wide variety of issues including national security.  He has chaired the Committee on International Security and Arms Control, and has been recognized by the [[Federation of American Scientists]] and the [[American Physical Society]] for shaping government policy.<ref name="DSC" /><ref name="fas"/><ref name="aps"/>

==Research==
Jeanloz was an early researcher in [[mineral physics]], and was one of those who proposed the field for recognition by the [[American Geophysical Union]] (AGU).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Liebermann |date=April 14, 2020 |first1=Robert Cooper |title=About - Mineral and Rock Physics - History of MRP section |url=https://connect.agu.org/mrp/about |website=American Geophysical Union.}}</ref> His work has connected mineral physics, chemistry, and materials science.<ref name="DSC" /><ref name="Macarthur"/>

{{quote|Nowadays, when people ask me, "What should I do?" I say, "Consider at least one possibility is to create a new field." &ndash; Raymond Jeanloz<ref name="Zierler"/>}}

Jeanloz studies processes that occur under high temperatures and pressures, conditions that are characteristic of the interiors of planets and the [[core-mantle boundary]] of the [[Earth]].<ref name="Sanders"/><ref name="Slesinger"/><ref name="Zierler"/><ref name="Carmichael"/> Jeanloz studies planetary interiors and the properties of materials at high pressures to characterize the processes by which planets evolve over geological time periods.<ref name="O'Neill"/><ref name="nas"/><ref name="Zierler"/><ref name="Carmichael"/> In the interiors of planets, pressure on materials can be millions of times higher than those at the Earth's surface and materials can behave in very different ways.<ref name="DSC" /> Jeanloz has examined the properties and state equations of materials including [[Alkali metal halide|alkali halides]], [[Alkaline earth metal|alkaline-earth monoxides]], [[silicate perovskite]] and [[iron]].<ref name="Carmichael" /> 

Jeanloz has created tools and experiments that enable him to recreate and study deep interior conditions in a laboratory setting, often by generating extremely high pressure in tiny amounts.<ref name="DSC" /><ref name="nas"/> He and his students have created new materials that can only be synthesized at extreme pressures, including ultra-hard diamond-like substances.<ref name="Macarthur"/> He has used diamond tips to simulate compression, creating [[Diamond anvil cell|diamond anvil cells]] capable of producing 4 to 5 million atmospheres, comparable to the pressures found at the center of the Earth.<ref name="SpaceNews2007">{{cite news |title=UV laser, diamond can generate pressures close to those in cores of supergiant planets |url=https://spacenews.com/uv-laser-diamond-can-generate-pressures-close-to-those-in-cores-of-supergiant-planets/ |work=SpaceNews |date=2 May 2007}}</ref> He has created impact waves by shooting projectiles at high speeds, and generated high-energy laser pulses.<ref name="DSC" /><ref name="nas"/> He has furthered the use of techniques for shock-loading, deformation, spectroscopy, and phase equilibria.<ref name="Carmichael"/> By combining dynamic laser-induced shock waves and static diamond anvils, Jeanloz has found ways to study the behavior of materials at pressures that could range from millions to billions of atmospheres. This allows scientists to simulate conditions within [[Giant planet|giant]] and [[Super-Jupiter|supergiant planets]].<ref name="SpaceNews2007" /><ref name="Fildes">{{cite news |last1=Fildes |first1=Jonathan |date=22 May 2009 |title=Man-made star to unlock cosmic secrets |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/8044620.stm |work=BBC News}}</ref>

His research has led to greater understanding of how planets form, the composition of their interiors, and how those interiors behave.<ref name="DSC" /><ref name="Cartier">{{cite news |last1=Cartier |first1=Kimberly M. S. |title=Remaking a Planet One Atom at a Time |url=https://eos.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Jul-20_mag.pdf |work=EOS|volume=101|issue=7|pages=30–35 |date=2020}}</ref>  His research group is best known for experiments documenting that [[bridgmanite]],<ref> The name Bridgmanite became official in 2014. Earlier publications use the name perovskite. {{cite web |title=Bridgmanite |url=https://www.mindat.org/min-45900.html |website=mindat.org |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref> a high-pressure form of {{chem2|(Mg,Fe)SiO3}}, is the primary material making up Earth's interior.<ref name="Macarthur" /><ref name="SpaceNews2007" />  He and his colleagues provided the first experimental determination of the temperature at Earth's center, concluding that it is as hot as the Sun's surface.<ref name="Macarthur"/> They also found evidence for chemical reactions between the rocky mantle and metallic core, likely making the core-mantle boundary one of Earth's most dynamic regions.<ref name="Macarthur" /><ref name="Sanders">{{cite news |last1=Sanders |first1=Robert |title=Glitches in the Earth's wobble help geophysicists probe the planet's core |url=https://spacenews.com/glitches-in-the-earths-wobble-help-geophysicists-probe-the-planets-core/ |access-date=29 July 2024 |work=SpaceNews |date=29 January 2001}}</ref><ref name="Slesinger">{{cite news |last1=Slesinger |first1=Audrey |title=News Notes -- Redefining the Core-Mantle Boundary |url=http://www.geotimes.org/jan01/earthsinterior.html |work=Geotimes |issue=January |date=2001}}</ref> 

Jeanloz' group and their collaborators have modeled processes of diamond formation, indicating that diamonds may be hailing inside "icy" giant planets like [[Neptune]].<ref name="Kraus">{{cite news |last1=Kraus |first1=Dominik |title=On Neptune, It's Raining Diamonds |url=https://www.americanscientist.org/article/on-neptune-its-raining-diamonds |access-date=6 August 2024 |work=American Scientist |date=6 August 2018 |language=en}}</ref>
They have helped characterize the primary constituents of giant planets and stars, the high-pressure fluid-metal forms of hydrogen and helium. They have determined that helium and hydrogen can form a metallic liquid alloy at the extreme pressures that occur at the cores of [[Jupiter]] and Saturn.<ref name="O'Neill">{{cite news |last1=O'Neill |first1=Ian |title=Could Jupiter and Saturn Contain Liquid Metal Helium? |url=https://www.universetoday.com/16533/could-jupiter-and-saturn-contain-liquid-metal-helium/ |access-date=29 July 2024 |work=Universe Today |date=8 August 2008}}</ref><ref name="Stevenson">{{cite journal |last1=Stevenson |first1=David J. |title=Metallic helium in massive planets |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=12 August 2008 |volume=105 |issue=32 |pages=11035–11036 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0806430105 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2008PNAS..10511035S |language=en |issn=0027-8424}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Jupiter and Saturn full of liquid metal helium |url=https://phys.org/news/2008-08-jupiter-saturn-full-liquid-metal.html |work=phys.org |date=August 6, 2008 |language=en}}</ref> They have studied pressurized hydrogen and documented an insulator-to-metal transition in fluid hydrogen, identifying the conditions under which it turns into a metal.<ref name="Bishop">{{cite news |last1=Bishop |first1=Breanna |title=NIF Reveals How Hydrogen Becomes Metallic in Giant Planets {{!}} National Ignition Facility & Photon Science |url=https://lasers.llnl.gov/news/nif-reveals-how-hydrogen-becomes-metallic-giant-planets |access-date=30 July 2024 |work=National Ignition Facility & Photon Science |date=August 17, 2018 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Robert">{{cite news |last1=Sanders |first1=Robert |title=Zapping hydrogen gas with 168 lasers turns it into a metal |url=https://news.berkeley.edu/2018/08/20/zapping-hydrogen-gas-with-168-lasers-turns-it-into-a-metal/ |work=Berkeley News |date=20 August 2018 |language=en}}</ref> Their research also suggests that helium separates out of fluid metallic hydrogen inside Jupiter and [[Saturn]], creating an [[Miscibility|immiscibility]] region in Jupiter and a four-layered planetary structure.<ref name="Lopatka">{{cite journal |last1=Lopatka |first1=Alex |title=Squeezed hydrogen and helium don't mix |journal=Physics Today |date=1 August 2021 |volume=74 |issue=8 |pages=18–19 |doi=10.1063/pt.3.4810 |bibcode=2021PhT....74h..18L  }}</ref>

In another collaboration Jeanloz has studied the behavior of a novel [[superionic ice|superionic form of water ice]], one that is simultaneously liquid and solid and can conduct electricity as if it was a metal. The mantles of ice giant planets like Uranus and Neptune may contain superionic ice, possibly explaining some odd behaviors of their magnetic fields.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=2018-02-05 |title=New Form of Water, Both Liquid and Solid, Is 'Really Strange' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/02/05/science/superionic-water-neptune-uranus.html |access-date=2024-07-30 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name="Fessenden">{{cite news |last=Fessenden |first=Maris |title=Scientists Make Weird Type of Ice Halfway Between Solid and Liquid |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/scientists-make-weird-ice-halfway-between-solid-and-liquid-180968053/ |work=Smithsonian Magazine |date=February 6, 2018 |language=en}}</ref>  His group's experiments have also pioneered the discovery of crystal instabilities causing strain-induced [[Metamictisation|amorphization]] and fracture-like processes, leading to new insights on how materials break.<ref name="Li">{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=B. Y. |last2=Li |first2=A. C. |last3=Zhao |first3=S. |last4=Meyers |first4=M. A. |title=Amorphization by mechanical deformation |journal=Materials Science and Engineering: R: Reports |date=1 June 2022 |volume=149 |article-number=100673 |doi=10.1016/j.mser.2022.100673 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0927796X22000122 |access-date=6 August 2024 |issn=0927-796X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Idrissi">{{cite journal |last1=Idrissi |first1=Hosni |last2=Carrez |first2=Philippe |last3=Cordier |first3=Patrick |title=On amorphization as a deformation mechanism under high stresses |journal=Current Opinion in Solid State and Materials Science |date=1 February 2022 |volume=26 |issue=1 |article-number=100976 |doi=10.1016/j.cossms.2021.100976 |bibcode=2022COSSM..26j0976I |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1359028621000796 |issn=1359-0286|hdl=20.500.12210/59104 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
